hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: You generate short codes by taking the first 7 characters of base62(MD5(longUrl)). What's the main problem at scale?
options: MD5 is too slow to compute per request
Truncated hashes collide, so you need collision detection and retry
Base62 can't represent MD5 output
Hash-based codes can't be stored in a database index
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: Truncating a hash to about 42 bits makes collisions likely as the table grows (birthday paradox), so you must check for an existing code and retry with a salt. MD5 is cheap to compute, and any bytes can be base62-encoded.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: Short codes come from a single auto-increment counter encoded in base62. Which concern is most significant?
options: Codes will collide frequently
Codes will be much longer than with hashing
Codes are sequential and guessable, and one counter is a bottleneck and single point of failure
Base62 encoding of integers is not reversible
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: A counter never collides and gives the shortest codes, but sequential IDs let people enumerate links, and a single counter must be made highly available and fast. Common fixes are counter ranges per server and shuffling/obfuscating IDs.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: How does a Key Generation Service (KGS) typically avoid handing the same key to two app servers?
options: Each app server hashes the URL and asks KGS to check it
KGS generates keys on demand using the current timestamp
App servers pick random keys and KGS rejects duplicates later
KGS pre-generates unique keys and atomically moves batches from 'unused' to 'used' before handing them out
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: A KGS pre-generates keys offline and hands out batches, marking them used atomically, so no two servers get the same key and no check is needed at write time. Random keys with later rejection is just collision handling moved elsewhere.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: With a KGS, each app server caches a batch of 1,000 keys in memory. An app server crashes. What happens?
options: Its unused keys are lost; that's acceptable given the huge keyspace
The same keys get issued to another server, causing duplicates
The KGS must roll back every URL created by that server
All servers must stop until the batch is recovered
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: Keys were marked used when handed out, so a crash just wastes the unused ones. With 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion keys that's negligible, and it's safer than risking reuse. They are never re-issued, which is the whole point of marking them used first.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: Product wants the same long URL to always return the same short code. Which approach supports this most directly?
options: A random KGS key per request
A global counter per request
Deterministic hashing of the long URL, or a lookup index on longUrl before creating
Snowflake IDs per request
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: Deduplication needs either a deterministic function of the URL (hash) or an index from longUrl to code that you check before creating a new one. Counters, KGS keys and Snowflake IDs all produce a new value per request.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: To avoid one central counter, each app server is assigned a range (server A gets 1–1M, B gets 1M–2M) from a coordinator like ZooKeeper. What's the main trade-off?
options: Codes can collide across servers
Codes are no longer roughly time-ordered globally, and unused range parts are wasted on crashes
The coordinator is called on every URL creation
Codes become much longer than a single counter's
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: Ranges remove the per-request bottleneck: the coordinator is only contacted when a range runs out. IDs from different servers interleave, so global ordering is lost, and a crashed server's unused range is skipped. Ranges never overlap, so there are no collisions.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: You use hash-based codes with collision retry: on collision you append a salt and rehash. Two requests for different URLs collide at the same moment. What's needed for correctness?
options: A larger hash function like SHA-512
A cache in front of the database
Retrying with exponential backoff only
An atomic insert-if-absent, such as a unique constraint on the short code
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: 'Check then insert' races: both requests can see the code as free. A unique index (or conditional put) makes the insert atomic, so one wins and the other gets an error and retries with a new salt. A bigger hash lowers the odds but doesn't remove the race.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: Which are advantages of a pre-generated KGS over hashing the long URL? Select all that apply.
options: No collision checks at write time
Keys can be non-sequential, so they're hard to guess
The same long URL automatically gets the same code
Key generation work happens offline, off the request path
No extra service to run and keep available
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: A KGS guarantees uniqueness up front, can hand out shuffled keys and moves work off the hot path. It doesn't dedupe identical URLs (each request gets a new key), and it's an extra component that must be highly available.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: Users can choose custom aliases (e.g. /my-sale) alongside generated codes. Which problems must you handle? Select all that apply.
options: A custom alias can clash with a code the generator will produce later
Reserved words such as /api or /admin must be blocked
Custom aliases make base62 encoding impossible
Racing requests for the same alias need an atomic uniqueness check
Custom aliases can't be cached
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: Aliases share the namespace with generated codes, so either reserve them in the KGS or keep separate namespaces, block route names, and enforce uniqueness atomically. Aliases are just keys, so they cache normally, and base62 still works for generated codes.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: A Snowflake-style 64-bit ID (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) encoded in base62 produces codes of about 11 characters, longer than a typical 7-character short code.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: True. 62^10 ≈ 8.4×10^17 is below 2^63 ≈ 9.2×10^18, while 62^11 is far above it, so large 64-bit IDs need about 11 base62 characters. That's why shorteners prefer compact counters or KGS keys.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: Using a cryptographic hash like SHA-256 and truncating it to 7 base62 characters eliminates collisions because SHA-256 is collision-resistant.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: False. Collision resistance applies to the full 256-bit output. Truncating to 7 base62 characters leaves about 42 bits, and by the birthday bound collisions become likely after a few million URLs.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: Why do URL shorteners commonly use base62 (0-9, a-z, A-Z) instead of base64?
options: Base62 produces shorter strings than base64
Base64's + and / characters aren't URL-safe without escaping
Base62 is faster to decode
Base64 can't encode integers
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: Standard base64 uses + and /, which have special meaning in URLs. Base62 only uses alphanumerics. Base64 is actually slightly denser (6 vs about 5.95 bits per char); base64url (- and _) is the other common choice.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: Roughly how many unique codes does a 7-character base62 code space provide?
options: About 3.5 trillion
About 56 billion
About 218 trillion
About 78 billion
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 ≈ 3.5 trillion. 56.8 billion is 62^6 and about 218 trillion is 62^8. At 100M new URLs/day, 3.5T lasts nearly 100 years.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: What does this base62 encoder print?
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: 61 is the last digit, 'Z'. 62 = 1×62 + 0, so it's '10' (most significant digit first). 3843 = 61×62 + 61, so it's 'ZZ', the largest 2-char value. '01' would come from forgetting to prepend.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: You expect 1 billion URLs in total over the service's life. What's the minimum base62 code length that can hold them all?
options: 5 characters
7 characters
6 characters
8 characters
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: 62^5 ≈ 916 million, just under 1 billion, while 62^6 ≈ 56.8 billion is enough. Many designs still pick 7 for headroom and so codes can be random rather than dense.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: A base62 short code is stored in MySQL with the default case-insensitive collation (utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci). What bug will appear?
options: Codes longer than 6 characters get truncated
Digits sort after letters, breaking range scans
Inserts fail because base62 contains non-ASCII characters
'abc' and 'ABC' are treated as equal, so lookups and uniqueness checks break
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: Base62 is case-sensitive: 'a' and 'A' are different digits. A case-insensitive collation makes 'abc' equal 'ABC', so a unique index rejects valid codes and lookups can return the wrong row. Use a binary or case-sensitive collation.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: Encoding counter value 125 in base62 gives '21'. What does the leftmost '2' represent?
options: The number of digits in the code
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: Positional base62: '21' = 2×62^1 + 1×62^0 = 124 + 1 = 125. Using base 10 place values would give 21, a common slip.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: Some shorteners drop look-alike characters (0/O, 1/l/I) from the alphabet, giving about base56. What's the trade-off?
options: Codes can no longer be decoded back to integers
Codes become easier to read and type but slightly longer for the same keyspace
Codes become shorter because the alphabet is smaller
The code space becomes unlimited
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: A smaller alphabet means fewer bits per character, so you need slightly longer codes for the same capacity, but humans make fewer transcription mistakes. Any alphabet with a fixed order still decodes back to an integer.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: You base62-encode an auto-increment ID directly. Which issues does this create? Select all that apply.
options: Codes reveal roughly how many links exist
Consecutive links have predictable codes that can be enumerated
Different IDs can map to the same code
Early codes are shorter than later ones unless padded
The encoding can't be reversed to recover the ID
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: Direct encoding is a bijection: no collisions and it's reversible. But it leaks volume, allows enumeration and gives variable length. Fixes include a reversible shuffle (e.g. a Feistel cipher over the ID) and padding.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: Which properties hold for base62 encoding of non-negative integers with a fixed alphabet order? Select all that apply.
options: Each integer has exactly one unpadded encoding
Decoding is the reverse of the repeated divide-by-62 process
It compresses arbitrary data to fewer bits than the input
Each character carries about 5.95 bits (log2 62)
It hides the original integer from anyone who knows the alphabet
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: Base62 is just positional notation: unique, reversible, about 5.95 bits per char. It isn't compression (no entropy is removed) and it isn't encryption: anyone with the alphabet can decode it.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: Base62-encoding a sequential ID makes short codes unpredictable, as long as the alphabet order is kept secret.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: False. A shuffled alphabet is a simple substitution: sequential IDs still give visibly related codes, and a handful of samples reveal the mapping. Use a proper keyed permutation or random keys if unpredictability matters.

hld-url-shortener:1.prompt: Going from 6 to 7 base62 characters multiplies the number of available codes by 62.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:1.explanation: True. Each extra position multiplies capacity by the base: 62^7 / 62^6 = 62, taking you from about 56.8 billion to about 3.5 trillion codes.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: Marketing needs accurate click counts for every visit to a short link. Which redirect status should the shortener return?
options: 301 Moved Permanently
308 Permanent Redirect
302 Found
304 Not Modified
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: Browsers can cache 301 (and 308) redirects and go straight to the destination on repeat visits, so your server never sees those clicks. 302 is temporary, so every visit comes back to you. 304 isn't a redirect at all.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: What's the main benefit of returning 301 for short links?
options: It lets you change the destination later without anyone noticing
It guarantees every click is logged
It prevents search engines from indexing the target
Browsers and caches can remember it, cutting load and latency on repeat visits
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: A permanent redirect is cacheable by default, so repeat visits skip your servers entirely. The flip side is exactly why it's bad for changing destinations or counting every click.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: Users can edit where a short link points. A few months after launch they complain that edits 'don't work' for some visitors. You've been returning 301. What's going on?
options: Visitors' browsers cached the old 301 and never ask your server again
Your database replica is lagging behind the primary
The CDN rejects 301 responses with long URLs
301 responses can't include a Location header
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: Browsers can cache 301s for a long time, so returning visitors follow the old target without contacting you. For editable links, use 302/307 or 301 with a short Cache-Control max-age. Replica lag would resolve in seconds, not months.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: A short link is used as the target of an HTML form POST, and the method must be preserved after the redirect. Which status code is correct for a temporary redirect?
options: 302 Found
307 Temporary Redirect
301 Moved Permanently
303 See Other
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: 307 requires the client to repeat the same method and body. Browsers historically turn POST into GET on 301/302, and 303 explicitly asks for a GET. 308 is the permanent version of 307.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: You want 302 semantics (every click reaches you) but also want a CDN to absorb most redirect traffic. What's a sensible approach?
options: Return 301 so the CDN caches it forever
Disable the CDN for redirect paths
Cache the redirect at the CDN briefly and log clicks from CDN edge logs or an edge function
Return 200 with a meta-refresh tag instead
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: A CDN can cache a 302 with s-maxage while edge logs or edge workers capture every click, so you keep analytics and offload origin. 301 loses browser-side clicks for good, and meta refresh is slower and worse for SEO and clients.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: How do search engines like Google generally treat a 301 compared with a 302?
options: They ignore 301s and only follow 302s
They penalise any site that uses 301
They treat both identically in all cases
A 301 signals the target is the canonical URL; a 302 suggests the original may come back
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: A 301 tells search engines the move is permanent, so they consolidate ranking signals on the destination. A 302 is a temporary move, so the original URL may stay indexed. Google says it handles both, but the signals differ.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: A shortener returns 301 with Cache-Control: max-age=300. What does a browser do on the next click 10 minutes later?
options: Contacts the shortener again, because the cached redirect expired
Uses the cached redirect forever, since 301 overrides Cache-Control
Shows an error because 301 can't carry Cache-Control
Follows the redirect but sends a POST
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: Explicit Cache-Control limits how long a 301 is cached; after 300 s the browser revalidates by requesting the short URL again. That's a way to keep some cacheability while still allowing edits and counting most clicks.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: Which statements about 301 vs 302 for a URL shortener are correct? Select all that apply.
options: 302 sends more traffic to your servers because browsers don't cache it by default
301 can cause click analytics to undercount returning visitors
302 makes changing the destination later safe
301 guarantees the redirect is never cached anywhere
302 always preserves POST bodies in all browsers
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: 302 isn't cached by default, so every click reaches you: more load, accurate analytics, editable targets. 301 is the opposite and is cached. Browsers commonly turn POST into GET on 302, which is why 307 exists.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: Which redirect codes tell the client to repeat the same HTTP method and body? Select all that apply.
options: 307 Temporary Redirect
302 Found
308 Permanent Redirect
303 See Other
301 Moved Permanently
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: 307 and 308 were added specifically to guarantee method and body are preserved. 301/302 allow clients to change POST to GET (and browsers do), and 303 explicitly requires a GET.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: Returning 302 for short links means browsers never cache the redirect, no matter what headers you send.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: False. A 302 isn't cached by default, but it becomes cacheable if you send explicit freshness headers like Cache-Control: max-age or Expires. The default behaviour is what matters for most shorteners.

hld-url-shortener:2.prompt: A 302 redirect adds one extra round trip to the shortener for every click compared with a cached 301.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:2.explanation: True. With a cached 301, repeat visits go straight to the destination. With a 302, the browser asks the shortener each time, which adds a round trip of latency and load in exchange for control and analytics.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: A shortener has about 100:1 read:write traffic. What should sit in front of the database for redirect lookups?
options: A write-back cache for new URLs
A message queue for redirect requests
A cache keyed by short code (e.g. Redis), filled via cache-aside
A full-text search index
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: Redirects are simple key lookups with a heavily skewed popularity distribution, a textbook fit for a cache-aside key-value cache. Queuing redirects would add latency, and full-text search is irrelevant to exact-key lookups.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: You estimate 20,000 redirects/s at peak, and the top 20% of links get 80% of traffic. Total mappings are 5 TB. What's a sensible cache sizing approach?
options: Cache all 5 TB so every lookup hits
Cache only the hot fraction (a small slice of the dataset) with LRU/LFU
Skip caching since the dataset is too big
Cache only links created in the last hour
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: With skewed traffic, caching a small hot fraction gives a high hit rate at a fraction of the cost. Caching all 5 TB in RAM is expensive for little extra benefit, and creation time is a poor proxy for popularity.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: Bots request millions of random short codes that don't exist. Your cache hit rate drops and DB load rises. What helps most?
options: Increase cache TTL for existing links
Use 301 instead of 302
Add more DB read replicas only
Cache 'not found' with a short TTL and/or check a Bloom filter of existing codes
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: This is cache penetration: unknown keys always miss. Negative caching or a Bloom filter answers 'doesn't exist' without the DB. Replicas absorb load but don't fix the waste, and the status code doesn't affect lookups for missing codes.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: A link is deleted for abuse, but users still get redirected to the malicious site for an hour. What's the most likely cause?
options: The cached mapping (Redis/CDN) wasn't invalidated when the link was deleted
The DB delete wasn't committed
Base62 decoding returns the wrong ID
LRU evicted the deletion record
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: Delete must also invalidate the cache and CDN (and ideally return 410). Otherwise the old mapping lives until its TTL expires. A one-hour delay matching a TTL points to caching, not the DB.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: A tweet with a short link goes viral: 500k requests/s for one code. Even Redis is struggling on the node that holds that key. What's the best next layer?
options: Shard the database by short code
Switch to write-through caching
Add an in-process cache on app servers and/or cache the redirect at the CDN edge
Lower the TTL of that key to 1 second
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: One key lives on one Redis node, so more shards don't help. An in-memory LRU on each app server and edge caching spread the load horizontally. A shorter TTL would just add misses.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: Which store characteristic best suits short code → long URL mappings at a scale of billions of rows?
options: Strong multi-row ACID transactions across tables
A horizontally scalable key-value or wide-column store with lookups by primary key
A graph database for link relationships
A time-series database
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: The access pattern is 'get by key', and writes are independent inserts, so a partitioned KV store (e.g. DynamoDB, Cassandra) scales simply. Cross-table transactions aren't needed for this workload. Sharded Postgres also works but needs more manual effort.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: Redirect latency p99 jumps every time a cache node restarts, as all its keys miss at once and the DB spikes. Which fix targets this directly?
options: Use 302 instead of 301
Remove the TTL from all keys
Increase the base62 code length
Warm the cache from a hot-key list before taking traffic, and coalesce concurrent misses
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: A cold cache node sends a burst of misses to the DB. Pre-warming with popular codes and request coalescing (single-flight per key) smooth the restart. Removing TTLs doesn't help because the keys are gone, not expired.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: Which make sense for the read path of a high-traffic URL shortener? Select all that apply.
options: CDN or edge caching of redirects for popular links
Cache-aside lookup in Redis keyed by short code
Reading from DB replicas on cache miss
Synchronously writing an analytics row to the main DB before redirecting
Locking the URL row for each redirect
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: Edge caching, a KV cache and replica reads all offload the primary. Synchronous analytics writes and row locks put write cost on every read and destroy redirect latency; analytics should be async.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: You read from DB replicas on cache miss. A user creates a link and clicks it immediately, getting a 404. Which fixes are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Write the new mapping into the cache at creation time
On a replica miss for a fresh code, fall back to the primary
Increase the cache TTL to 30 days
Route reads from the creating user to the primary for a short window
Switch the redirect code from 302 to 301
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: The 404 comes from replica lag. Populating the cache on write, falling back to the primary on miss, or read-your-writes routing all fix it. TTL length and redirect status don't help a code that isn't on the replica yet.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: Because short-link mappings rarely change once created, they can usually be cached with long TTLs as long as deletes and edits explicitly invalidate the cache.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: True. Mappings are effectively immutable, so long TTLs are safe and give high hit rates, provided edits, deletes and abuse takedowns invalidate the cache and CDN explicitly.

hld-url-shortener:3.prompt: With a 99% cache hit rate, the database still sees about half of redirect traffic, since misses are expensive.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:3.explanation: False. A 99% hit rate means only 1% of lookups reach the DB, e.g. 200/s out of 20,000/s. Each miss costs more than a hit, but the request count to the DB is still just 1% of total.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Where should click analytics be recorded so they don't slow down redirects?
options: Inside a DB transaction before sending the redirect
Emitted asynchronously (e.g. to Kafka) and processed off the request path
In the browser using localStorage
By re-running the redirect query with an extra UPDATE
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: Redirects should be as fast as possible. Fire-and-forget events to a log or queue let consumers aggregate later. A synchronous DB write adds latency and couples redirects to analytics DB health.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: You count clicks with UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1 WHERE code = $1 on every redirect. A viral link makes the DB slow for everyone. Why?
options: UPDATE statements can't use indexes
The clicks column overflows past 2^31
Every redirect contends for the same row lock, serialising writes on that link
PostgreSQL disallows UPDATE during reads
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: All increments hit one row, so they queue behind a single row lock and generate heavy write/WAL traffic. Buffer counts (in memory or Redis) or stream events and aggregate in batches. The UPDATE does use the index on code.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Analytics must show unique visitors per link per day across billions of clicks, with about 1% error acceptable. Which data structure fits best?
options: HyperLogLog per link per day
A set of all visitor IDs per link
A Bloom filter per link
A sorted set of timestamps
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts with about 0.8% standard error in roughly 12 KB (as in Redis), regardless of cardinality. Exact sets grow with visitors. Bloom filters answer membership, not counts.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Kafka gives at-least-once delivery to your click consumer. After a consumer restart, click counts are inflated. What's the best fix?
options: Switch Kafka to at-most-once and accept losses
Retry failed messages more aggressively
Add more partitions to the topic
Give each click an event ID and make aggregation idempotent (dedupe or commit offsets with results atomically)
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: At-least-once means replays after restarts. Dedupe by event ID, or store consumer offsets in the same transaction as the aggregates, so reprocessing doesn't double-count. At-most-once trades duplicates for silent loss.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Dashboards query 'clicks per hour by country for link X over 90 days'. Which storage fits that query pattern best?
options: The same row-store table that holds URL mappings
A columnar OLAP store (e.g. ClickHouse) with pre-aggregated rollups
Redis strings keyed by link
An object store with one file per click, scanned at query time
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: Analytical group-by queries over time ranges suit columnar stores and rollup tables. Running them on the OLTP mapping table competes with redirects, and scanning one file per click is far too slow.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Your click stream aggregates by event time into hourly windows. Mobile clients send events up to 10 minutes late. What should the stream processor do?
options: Drop any event that arrives after its window closes
Use processing time instead so lateness doesn't matter
Use watermarks with allowed lateness, updating windows as late events arrive
Wait 24 hours before emitting any result
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: Watermarks with allowed lateness keep windows open long enough for typical delays and then finalise. Processing time puts late events in the wrong hour, dropping them loses data, and waiting a day makes dashboards useless.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: A redirect service publishes click events to Kafka, but the Kafka cluster is down. What's the best behaviour for the redirect path?
options: Still redirect; buffer events locally or drop them, and alert
Return 503 until Kafka recovers
Block the redirect until the publish succeeds
Write each event synchronously to the main URL database instead
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: Redirects are the core product; analytics is secondary. Degrade gracefully with a bounded local buffer (or drop and count the losses). Failing or blocking redirects turns an analytics outage into a full outage.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Which steps belong in a URL shortener's click analytics pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: Emit an event with code, timestamp, referrer and user agent
Enrich events (e.g. IP to country, UA to device) in a consumer
Filter or flag bot traffic before reporting
Block the redirect until the event is stored in the warehouse
Roll up raw events into time-bucketed aggregates
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: Emit, enrich, filter bots and roll up is the standard flow. Waiting for warehouse storage puts analytics latency on every redirect.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Raw click events for 3 years would be about 500 TB. Which strategies keep cost under control? Select all that apply.
options: Keep raw events briefly, then keep only hourly/daily rollups
Move old raw data to cheap object storage in a compressed columnar format
Store every event in Redis for fast queries
Sample very high-volume links for non-billing metrics
Duplicate events into the OLTP database for backup
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: Tiered retention, compressed cold storage and sampling all reduce cost while keeping useful metrics. Keeping 500 TB in Redis memory or duplicating it into OLTP is extremely expensive.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Counting clicks at the CDN edge from access logs can work even when redirects are cached at the edge and never reach your origin.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: True. Edge logs record every request the CDN serves, including cache hits, so you can ship them into your pipeline. That lets you cache redirects at the edge without losing click data, though logs arrive with some delay.

hld-url-shortener:4.prompt: Real-time per-second click counters on a dashboard require every event to be written to the warehouse before it's displayed.
options: True
False
hld-url-shortener:4.explanation: False. A common split is a fast path (stream processing or Redis counters) for near-real-time numbers and a batch path into the warehouse for accurate historical reports. The dashboard reads the fast path.
